name: Pleistocene Canis Proximal Phalanx UW57662
description: This 3D model represents UW-57662, a proximal phalanx (the first bone of a toe) from the genus Canis, discovered in 2022 at Natural Trap Cave (on Bureau of Land Managment land, and curated at the University of Wyoming).  The bone dates to the Pleistocene and may belong to either a wolf or a coyote—distinguishing between the two is challenging because research from Natural Trap Cave has shown that Ice Age coyotes were significantly larger than their modern counterparts, creating strong overlap with wolves. Natural Trap Cave itself is an 85-foot limestone pit near the Bighorn Mountains that acted as a natural animal trap for tens of thousands of years, preserving an exceptional record of Ice Age fauna. This specimen is part of that rich archive of Wyoming’s Pleistocene predators.

name: Low Poly Deinocheirus
description:
Deinocheirus Mirificus: “unusual horrible hand”

Dinosaur from Mongolian Nemegt Formation of Late Cretaceous, well known for its at the time unusual arms and history in paleontologic research. Its original remains, found in 1970, were only the strange arms, leaving the rest of the body unknown. Various reconstructions portrayed it as a predator, creature similar to Therizinosaurs and so on.

In 2013 however, true form was figured out, thanks to more fossil material restored from the grip of fossil poachers. Skull, bodyplan and even likely diet was described.

Stomach content of Deinocheirus is made from gastrolits and fish remains, making it likely an omnivore, feeding on both animals and plants, given to its skull shape, related dinosaurs and weak bite force.

name: Green Sea Turtle: Fibropapillomatosis Disease
description:
**3D Model and Poster:
© 2024 David Nahabedian MSMI CMI at St. George's University**


**Background:**
Fibropapillomatosis (FP) is a common and contagious disease affecting **endangered green sea turtles (Chelonia mydas)** that produces large superficial tumors somtimes resulting in debilitation and death. In some turtle populations, upwards of 70 percent can be infected. The mouth, eyes, neck, tail, genitals and armpits are the most common sites for tumors to appear and grow. As they proliferate on the body, vital functions for survival are affected like sight, eating and swimming. In some cases, turtles grow tumors internally.

**Research Goal:**
Our research aimed to create a realistic and interactive 3D model depicting a case of FP in a green sea turtle using 3D scanning for veterinary students and educators.

Procedures approved within IACUC-24008-R
